title: A pgrep wait loop matches its own command line and waits for itself
claim: A shell loop that polls `pgrep -f <pattern>` to wait for a job cannot terminate when the pattern appears literally in its own command line, and the symptom is indistinguishable from the job still running.
appliesTo: Any `pgrep -f` or `pkill -f` invocation whose pattern is a literal substring of the command line issuing it — wait loops, cleanup steps, and process-liveness checks written inline rather than against a recorded PID.
expectation: `pgrep -f foo` reports whether the job matching foo is alive, so `until ! pgrep -f foo; do sleep; done` returns once the job exits.
reality: The waiting shell's own command line contains the pattern, so pgrep matches the waiter and reports a live process forever. Nothing errors and nothing hangs in a way a timeout will catch quickly: the loop keeps polling, the job it was watching finished long ago, and the only visible symptom is a long-running wait — exactly what a wait on a slow job looks like. `pkill -f` fails the same way in the other direction, killing the shell that issued it along with the target.
mechanism: `-f` matches against the full command line rather than the process name, and a shell running an inline loop has the entire loop, pattern included, in its own argv. Every poll therefore has at least one guaranteed match. The classic `ps | grep` version of this is well known and usually visible, because the grep appears in the output being read; here the output is discarded and only the exit status is consulted, so the extra match is never seen.
workaround: Wait on a PID rather than a pattern: capture `$!` and use `wait`, or poll `kill -0 "$pid"`. Where a pattern is unavoidable, break the literal so it cannot match itself — `pgrep -f 'agent-trial[.]ts'` matches the target's `agent-trial.ts` while the waiter's own argv contains the brackets and does not match. Before trusting any such loop, run the pattern once by hand and count the matches: a wait that has never been observed returning is not known to return.

evidence.command: until ! pgrep -f "agent-trial.ts clock" >/dev/null; do sleep 20; done
evidence.output: (never returns; the trial had already finished)
evidence.note: Hit three times in one session. The first cost an entire background wait that outlived the job it watched; the third was a `pkill -f "until ! pgrep"` meant to clean up the second, which terminated the foreground shell that issued it — exit 144.

check.confirmedIf: exit 0 — pgrep matched a pattern that appears only in its own command line
check.refutedIf: exit 1 — pgrep did not match itself

observations.note: Diagnosed once, then repeated twice more in the same session, which is the reason it is written down rather than remembered. The first instance was found only by listing the processes by hand after the wait had outlasted any plausible runtime for the job; nothing about the loop's behaviour distinguished it from a slow job. The third instance inverted it: a pkill intended to clear the second waiter matched the shell issuing it and killed that too.
